summary: Isaiah and Job describe the damage a moth does to a garment. Hosea uses that slow destruction to describe what Ephraim faces. The verb describes a sufferer whose eyes and bones waste away.

senses.definition: An insect whose young eat holes in clothing.

evidence.note: Those who condemn the speaker wear out like a garment eaten by a moth.
The moth eats a garment, in parallel with the grub eating wool.
Yahweh compares himself to a moth to Ephraim and to rot to Judah.
Under divine rebuke a person’s treasured possession wastes away as if consumed by a moth.
Eliphaz invokes the moth in describing the frailty of those who dwell in houses of clay.
Job compares decay to a garment a moth has eaten.
The moth’s house and a watchman’s hut illustrate how precarious the house of the wicked is.

words.summary: Grief takes its toll on the body. Its link with the noun for the insect is uncertain.

senses.definition: Lose strength or vitality under prolonged distress. The sufferer speaks first of an eye growing weak with grief, then of failing strength and wasting bones.

evidence.note: The preceding verse describes the speaker weeping through the night.
The same verb applies first to the eye and then to the bones, beside the failing of strength.

cognates.note: The sense of bodily decline fits the verb. The initial consonant differs from that of the Arabic word for moth.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2229, art. غث, form I (n31441)
evidence.note: Said of flesh becoming lean and of a sheep or goat becoming weak.

note: Job 9:9 names a constellation alongside Orion and the Pleiades. The Aramaic grass in Daniel 4–5 belongs to a separate word. In Matthew 6:19 the Peshitta uses a different Syriac word for moth, ܣܣܐ. The Arabic comparison for the verb would distinguish its initial consonant from that of the moth. The Hebrew contexts establish wasting away but cannot decide the historical relationship.
